planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; like the species, Little Redhead resents root disturbance once settled, so choose its permanent spot at planting time.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to light shade; Little Redhead is a Juniper Level Botanic Garden/Plant Delights Nursery selection of the native woodland wildflower Indian pink, chosen from a wild population for producing noticeably more flowering stems per clump and a longer bloom window than typical seed-grown plants. Each stem carries the same brilliant red, yellow-tipped tubular flowers that make the species one of the best native hummingbird plants for shaded gardens, but Little Redhead's heavier flower count makes it showier in smaller garden spaces. It is slow to bulk up the first year or two after transplanting but becomes long-lived and reliably floriferous once established, and it combines well with ferns, wild ginger, and woodland phlox.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or early fall in full sun and well-drained, sandy or loamy soil; established clumps tolerate the heat and humidity of Southeastern summers but decline quickly in soggy winter soil, so good drainage is essential.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; Peachie's Pick is a widely grown selection of the Southeastern native Stokes' aster, chosen for flower heads that run noticeably larger than the species — frequently 4 to 5 inches across — in a rich periwinkle-blue and for a more vigorous, floriferous clump. Blooms open over a long stretch from early summer into fall, especially with regular deadheading, and the sturdy stems hold up well for cutting. Native to wet pine savannas and coastal plain flatwoods, Stokes' aster and its cultivars handle heat and humidity better than most blue-flowered perennials, and Peachie's Pick is a reliable choice for southern pollinator borders.

common_name: Mary Gregory Stokes' Aster (Yellow Stoke's Aster)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or early fall in full sun and well-drained soil; give Mary Gregory the same lean, sandy to loamy conditions the species prefers, since wet winter soil is the most common cause of failure.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy or loamy soil; Mary Gregory is a soft pale-yellow-flowered selection of the native Southeastern Stokes' aster, a color that is unusual for this genus since almost all Stokesia cultivars in commerce are shades of blue, lavender, or white. The compact clumps produce cornflower-shaped blooms from early summer into fall and stay noticeably tidier and lower-growing than many blue-flowered forms, making it useful for edging a sunny border. Like the species, it is native to coastal plain flatwoods and pine savannas and tolerates Southeastern heat and humidity far better than most yellow-flowered perennials of similar bloom form, while remaining a strong draw for bees and butterflies.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in lean, well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun; like the species, Fireworks spreads gradually by rhizomes and flowers best when kept on the dry, lean side rather than in rich, moist beds.

directions: Plant in full sun in lean, well-drained soil; Fireworks (also sold under its German name, 'Fyrverkeri') is the most widely grown named cultivar of the native eastern sundrops, selected for a more compact habit than the species and for the vivid contrast between its wine-red flower buds and stems and the clear butter-yellow, day-opening flowers that follow. Bloom is heaviest from late spring into midsummer, and the reddish stems and buds keep the plant ornamentally interesting even between flushes. As with the species, rich or consistently moist soil produces weak, floppy growth, so Fireworks performs best in the same dry, sunny, low-fertility conditions favored by prairie and meadow wildflowers, and it is a reliable draw for bees.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

planting.note: Set out in spring with the crown planted a couple of inches deep and the roots shaded by low companion plants, training the twining stems up an obelisk, wire trellis, or fence in full sun.

directions: Grow on a narrow support such as an obelisk or wire trellis in full sun, keeping the roots cool and shaded beneath low underplanting; Princess Diana is one of the best-known hybrid offspring of the Texas native clematis, bred for flowers that open wider into a bright, tulip-like cerise-pink cup rather than the tightly closed urn shape of the wild species. It flowers prolifically from midsummer into fall on new growth, so cut the vine back hard to a foot or so above ground each late winter to keep it vigorous and well shaped. Like its Texas parent, it tolerates heat and dry spells better than most large-flowered clematis, making it a dependable choice for sunny southern gardens.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or early spring on dry, lean, well-drained soil; like the species, Red Midget flowers reliably from first-year seedlings and prefers poor soil, since excess fertility leads to weak stems and fewer blooms.

directions: Plant in full sun in dry, lean, well-drained soil; Red Midget is a compact seed strain of prairie coneflower bred to stay under a foot and a half tall — well under half the height of the straight species — while keeping the same tall thimble-shaped central cone and drooping ray petals. Its ray petals are a more uniform deep mahogany-red than the often two-toned yellow-and-red species, giving the flowers a richer, solid color from a distance. The dwarf habit resists flopping and suits front-of-border and container plantings where the taller species would need staking, while retaining the drought tolerance, deer resistance, and pollinator appeal that make prairie coneflower a staple of native meadow gardens.

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall on a fence, mailbox post, or trellis in moist, well-drained soil; give it full sun for the heaviest bloom, though it tolerates part shade with some reduction in flowering.

directions: Plant in full sun to light part shade in moist, well-drained soil on a sturdy trellis or fence; Alabama Crimson was selected from a wild Southeastern population for flower color that runs a truer, deeper red than most coral honeysuckle cultivars, which tend toward orange-red or coral. Whorled clusters of narrow red trumpets with yellow-orange throats open heavily in spring and continue with strong repeat flushes into fall, making it one of the longest-blooming coral honeysuckle selections for hummingbird gardens. It twines lightly and benefits from wire or lattice to grip, and like other native honeysuckle selections it is non-invasive and needs only light shaping after each bloom flush.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
